main.text: [III, 365] [col. 510] Chapter XI.
Some passages on the honey-making of bees which the Greek Fathers cite as if from Scripture.

Bees are commended above all for their skill in making honey. On this, in the sacred text of the Hebrews, [col. 511] you will find only Iud. XIV, 8: And behold, a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey! A swarm of bees, and honey: that is, a swarm of honey-making bees, or of bees producing honey, by the figure ἓν διὰ δυοῖν [hen dia dyoin]. But the Greek Fathers bring out three other texts from their own store. The first is Psalmi CXVII, (Hebraeis CXVIII,) 12: Ἐκύκλωσάν με, ὡσεὶ μέλισσαι κηρίον· [Ekyklōsan me, hōsei melissai kērion] They surrounded me, as bees a honeycomb. So Augustine, Jerome and Theodoret cite it from the Greek version. Nor do our editions have anything else. The Ethiopic also follows the same. And the Arabic, which I have in manuscript, reads احتاطوا بي مثل النحل بالشهد [iḥtāṭū bī mithl al-naḥl bi-l-shahd] They surrounded me, as bees a honeycomb. But for الشهد [al-shahd], that is, honeycomb, the printed editions have الشمع [al-shamʿ] wax, as if the Arabs had read κηρὸν [kēron] in the Greek, not κηρίον [kērion]. In the Hebrew, however, one reads only סבוני כדבורים, They surrounded me, like bees. And that κηρίον [kērion] seems to have been wrongly added. For David is speaking of his enemies; and he does not compare them with bees that surround a honeycomb, since there is nothing hostile in that, but with bees that surround a man or a beast in a body, to sting with hostile stings. So in Statius, Thebaid book 10:

So, when a shepherd, about to plunder them, has driven the armed bees from their pumice cave, the fierce cloud roars, and they urge one another on with buzzing, and all fly into the face of the foe. — — —
But these matters have already been dealt with above.

[III, 366] The second text is Prov. VI, 8, where, after the much-celebrated (πολυθρύλλητον [polythryllēton]) passage on the ant, Go to the ant, O sluggard, etc., the Greek edition reads: Ἢ πορεύθητι πρὸς τὴν μέλισσαν, καὶ μάθε, ὡς ἐργάτις ἐστι, τήν τε ἐργασίαν ὡς σεμνὴν ποιεῖται· ἧς τοὺς πόνους βασιλεῖς καὶ ἰδιῶται πρὸς ὑγίειαν προσφέρονται. ποθεινὴ δέ ἐστι πᾶσι, καὶ ἐπίδοξος· καίπερ οὖσα τῇ ῥώμῃ ἀσθενὴς, τὴν σοφίαν τιμήσασα προήχθη. [Ē poreuthēti pros tēn melissan, kai mathe, hōs ergatis esti, tēn te ergasian hōs semnēn poieitai; hēs tous ponous basileis kai idiōtai pros hygieian prospherontai. potheinē de esti pasi, kai epidoxos; kaiper ousa tē rhōmē asthenēs, tēn sophian timēsasa proēchthē.] Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)] rendered this in his version as follows: Or go to the bee, and learn how industrious she is, and how majestic a work she carries on: by whose labours both kings and private persons are wholesomely fed. And she is beloved and renowned among all; and, although weak in strength, she has nevertheless advanced by her zeal for wisdom. The Arabic version also: او انهب الي النحلة واعرف انها مثل الفاعل هي تعمل صناعتها طرفة عجيبة * واتعابها تحمل الي الملوك * والعامة يستعملوها لحفظ الصحة * وهي عند جميع الناس ماثورة مشرفة * مع ضعيفة في قوتها قدمت لانها اكرمت بالحكمة وفضلت * [aw inhab ilá al-naḥla wa-iʿrif annahā mithl al-fāʿil hiya taʿmal ṣināʿatahā ṭurfa ʿajība * wa-atʿābuhā tuḥmal ilá al-mulūk * wa-al-ʿāmma yastaʿmilūhā li-ḥifẓ al-ṣiḥḥa * wa-hiya ʿinda jamīʿ al-nās maʾthūra musharrafa * maʿa ḍaʿīfa fī quwwatihā qaddamat li-annahā ukrimat bi-l-ḥikma wa-fuḍḍilat *] Or go to the bee, and know that, like a workman, she fashions her work with wonderful art. And her labours are carried to kings, and the common people use them to preserve health. And she is excellent and noble among all men. Although she is weak in strength, she nevertheless excels, because she is commended for wisdom, [col. 512] and is outstanding. Many ancient writers cite the same passage: thus Clement of Alexandria, book 1 of the Stromata; Origen on Numbers, Homily 27, and on Isaiah, Homily 2; Basil on the Hexaemeron, Homily 8; Ambrose on the Hexaemeron, book 5, ch. 21; Jerome on Ezekiel, ch. 3; Theodoret, On Providence, Oration 5; Antiochus, Abbot of Saba, Homily 36; John of Damascus, book 2 of the Parallels, ch. 89. Yet, as Jerome rightly observes in the place cited, the Hebrew copies do not have this. Accordingly there is no trace of this passage in the Chaldee, the Syriac or the Vulgate version. And I have often wondered where the Greek translators took it from, as also certain other things which they insert here and there in various places. For it is not credible that they would have added these things of their own accord, unless they had found them already inserted in some copies of the Hebrews.

However that may be, certain points should be noted in this passage about the bee. First: the bee is joined with the ant, as is common among writers. Thus the Philosopher, History book 1, ch. 1, after saying that the bee and the ant are political and gregarious animals, adds: τὸ τῶν μελιττῶν γένος εἶναι ὑφ᾽ ἡγεμόνα· μύρμηκες δὲ, καὶ μυρία ἄλλα ἄναρχα [to tōn melittōn genos einai hyph᾽ hēgemona; myrmēkes de, kai myria alla anarcha], the race of bees is under a leader, but ants and countless others are without a leader. And book 9, ch. 38: Τῶν δ᾽ ἐντόμων ζώων ἐργατικώτατα σχεδόν ἐστι, καὶ πρός τ᾽ ἄλλα συγκρίνεσθαι πάντα, τότε τῶν μυρμήκων γένος, καὶ τὸ τῶν μελιττῶν [Tōn d᾽ entomōn zōōn ergatikōtata schedon esti, kai pros t᾽ alla synkrinesthai panta, tote tōn myrmēkōn genos, kai to tōn melittōn]: Of insect [III, 367] animals the most industrious, and to be preferred to all the rest, are the races of ants and of bees. Cicero, Academic Questions book 4: Whose (God's) majesty you bring down even to the perfection of bees and ants. Plutarch, in the book Whether an Old Man Should Engage in Public Affairs: Τὸ κοινωνικὸν, καὶ πολιτικὸν, ὃ καὶ μύρμηξιν ἄχρι τέλους παραμένει καὶ μελίτταις [To koinōnikon, kai politikon, ho kai myrmēxin achri telous paramenei kai melittais]: The communal and political life, in which both ants and bees remain to the very end. Aelian, History book 5, ch. 49: Μέλιτται, μύρμηκές τε, καὶ ἐκείνοις, ἐκφορᾶς νεκρῶν μέλειν ἡ σοφωτάτη φύσις ἔδωκεν [Melittai, myrmēkes te, kai ekeinois, ekphoras nekrōn melein hē sophōtatē physis edōken]: To bees and ants most wise nature has granted that they carry out their dead. Phocylides, or whoever he is, after describing the ant at some length, immediately adds about the bee:
Κάμνει δ' ἠερόφοιτος ἀριστοπόνος τε μέλισσα, [Kamnei d' ēerophoitos aristoponos te melissa,]

The airy, industrious bee also labors. Celsus, in Origen, foolishly asserts that man does not differ from the brutes on the ground that he has founded cities and uses civil government, καὶ γὰρ μύρμηκες, καὶ αἱ μέλισσαι [kai gar myrmēkes, kai hai melissai], for ants and bees do the same. But Origen refutes him thoroughly in book 4. Tertullian, book 1 Against Marcion, ch. 14: Imitate, if you can, the buildings of the bee, the stables of the ant, etc. Pontanus, book 1 On the Stars:
Alone, fearing winter, the ant stores in hollow pumice the wheaten labors it has plundered from men. The same love and the same skill belong to the thrifty bees.
Scaliger [=J. C. Scaliger, Exercitationes (1557)], in the poem entitled Avaricious Warfare:
The ant and the bee both lay up for the year. Diligence makes the one, zeal the other, manly. For this a hive, for that a tiny hollow is enough.
And in the one entitled Labor, the Father of Enjoyment:
The ant and the bee, workers, will teach us to labor for our share, then to enjoy our labor.

2. Nor is it contrary to the custom of Scripture that examples for life are sought from brute animals: as from the ant in the same verse; from the ox and the ass, Isa 1:3; from the turtledove, crane and swallow, Ierem. VIII, 7.; from serpents and doves, Matth. X, 16. In this way God sends down to a lower class, namely to the school of the brutes, those who have made no progress in his own school. 3. This too is commonplace, that the bee is set before men for imitation. Seneca, Epistle 84: We ought, as they say, to imitate the bees, which wander about and pluck the flowers suitable for making honey, then arrange whatever [col. 513] they have brought and distribute it through the honeycombs, etc. Lucretius, book 3: [III, 368] As bees in flowery glades sip at everything, so we likewise feed upon all your golden words,
Horace, book 4, Ode 2:
— — — I, after the manner and fashion of the Matine bee, that gathers the pleasing thyme with much labor, around the grove and the banks of moist Tibur, small as I am, fashion laborious songs.

More of this kind from Plato, Plutarch, Lucian and others are familiar to everyone. Nor do those who imagine that a thrifty woman was born from a bee mean anything else, as Simonides in Stobaeus, chapter 71:

Τὴν δ᾽ ἐκ μελίσσης, τήν τις εὐτυχεῖ λαβών· [Tēn d᾽ ek melissēs, tēn tis eutychei labōn;] Κείνῃ γὰρ οἴῃ μῶμος οὐ προσιζάνει· [Keinē gar oiē mōmos ou prosizanei;] Θάλλει δ᾽ ὑπ᾽ αὐτῆς κἀπαέξεται βίος. [Thallei d᾽ hyp᾽ autēs kapaexetai bios.]
He who has married one born from the bee is fortunate: for in her alone no fault resides; and the household flourishes and is increased by her. And Phocylides:
— — — ἡ δὲ μελίσσης [hē de melissēs] Οἰκονόμος τ᾽ ἀγαθὴ, καὶ ἐπίσταται ἐργάζεσθαι, [Oikonomos t᾽ agathē, kai epistatai ergazesthai,]

But she who is born of the bee is well versed in household management and knows how to work. Hence in Xenophon's Oeconomicus, chapter 13, ἡ τῶν μελισσῶν ἡγεμῶν [hē tōn melissōn hēgemōn], the leader of the bees, is compared at length with the mother of a household. Accordingly, even illustrious women did not disdain to be called by the name of bee: as among the Hebrews there are two named DEBORA: one, the nurse of Rebecca, Gen. XXXV, 8, and the other, the prophetess who judged Israel, Iudicum IV, 4. And among the Greeks there is MELISSA, the nymph who nursed Jupiter; and MELISSA, daughter of Epidamnus, of whom Stephanus speaks under Δυῤῥάχιον [Dyrrhachion]; and MELISSA, wife of Periander, king of the Corinthians; and a later MELISSA, whose Letter Aldus published in the volume of Greek Letters. 4. It is also an accepted usage that the bee is called ἐργάτις [ergatis], craftswoman or worker. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 40: Εἰσὶ δ᾽ αἱ μικραὶ ἐργάτιδες μᾶλλον τῶν μεγάλων [Eisi d' hai mikrai ergatides mallon tōn megalōn]. Similar to this is Varro, Rustica, book 3, chapter 16: The wild ones are smaller in size, and hairy, but better workers. And in Anthologia, book 1, chapter 60, bees are called in Antiphilus

Αἰθερίου πτηναὶ νέκταρος ἐργάτιδες [Aitheriou ptēnai nektaros ergatides], winged craftswomen of heavenly nectar. [III, 369] Not to mention Lucian, who in the Halcyon calls the bee μέλιτος ἐργάτιν [melitos ergatin], as also Pisides calls her τὴν σοφὴν τὴν ἐργάτιν [tēn sophēn tēn ergatin]. 5. But no one else, so far as I know, has called their ἐργασίαν σεμνὴν [ergasian semnēn]. Ambrose renders this venerable operation, Jerome chaste work, Castalio august work, Godefridus Tilmannus work full of cleanliness and honesty. I would prefer precious work or wonderful work, because it fits the matter better; and the old lexicographers teach that σεμνὸν [semnon] or σεπτὸν [septon] is taken in this sense. Hesychius: Σεμνή· (read Σεμνὰ) τίμια, σώφρων [Semnē (Semna): timia, sōphrōn]. The same: Σεπτά· θαυμαστά [Septa: thaumasta]. Following this, the Arabic version here has that the bee makes her work عجيبة طرفة [ʿajība ṭurfa], with wonderful art. (Wrongly printed طرقة [ṭrqa].) What if one were to read σμήνων [smēnōn] for σεμνὴν [semnēn], thus: τήν τε ἐργασίαν σμήνων ὡς ποιεῖται [tēn te ergasian smēnōn hōs poieitai], and how she does the work of the hives, that is, that wonderful work which is done in hives? This is a great secret of nature, and not yet sufficiently understood. The Philosopher, in the place cited above: Ὅταν δὲ εἰς σμῆνος ἀφίκωνται ἀποσείονται, καὶ ἀκολουθοῦσιν ἑκάστῃ τρεῖς, ἢ τέτταρες. τὸ δὲ λαμβανόμενον οὐ ῥᾴδιόν ἐστιν ἰδεῖν, οὐδὲ τὴν ἐργασίαν, ὅν τινα τρόπον ποιοῦνται, οὐκ ὦπται· [Hotan de eis smēnos aphikōntai aposeiontai, kai akolouthousin hekastē treis, ē tettares. to de lambanomenon ou rhadion estin idein, oude tēn ergasian, hon tina tropon poiountai, ouk ōptai] When they return to the hive (from gathering flowers), they shake themselves off, and each bee is followed by three or four. But what they receive is not easy to see. Nor has it yet been observed how they do their work. Worth knowing, if only it is true, is what Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] and Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] report about this, [col. 514] وقد صنع ارسطاطاليس لها بيتا من زجاج لينظر الي كيفية ما تصنع فابت ان تعمل حتي لطخته من باطن الزجاج بالطين [wa-qad ṣanaʿa Arisṭāṭālīs lahā baytan min zujāj li-yanẓura ilā kayfiyyat mā taṣnaʿ fa-abat an taʿmal ḥattā laṭṭakhathu min bāṭin al-zujāj bi-l-ṭīn] Aristotle made them a glass hive, in order to look in and see how they set about their work. But they refused to do any work until they had smeared the inside of the glass with mud. 6. There follows in the sacred text: Ἧς τοὺς πόνους βασιλεῖς καὶ ἰδιῶται πρὸς ὑγίειαν προσφέρονται· [Hēs tous ponous basileis kai idiōtai pros hygieian prospherontai] whose labours kings and private persons use for health. The labours of the bee, that is, honey: as in Hesiod's well-known line on drones, Works, line 303.
Οἵ τε μελισσάων κάματον τρύχουσιν ἀεργοὶ, [Hoi te melissaōn kamaton trychousin aergoi]
And who, idle, consume the labour of the bees. And in Euripides, Iphigenia in Tauris, there is reckoned among the funeral offerings
— — — — ξουθᾶν πόνημα μελισσᾶν, [xouthan ponēma melissan]

the labour of the tawny bees. Hence the proverb about a young man who wastes time uselessly explaining something commonly known: Σύγγνωθι τῷ μειρακίῳ τὸ μέλι πόνον μελίττης κηρύττοντι [Syngnōthi tō meirakiō to meli ponon melittēs kēryttonti], Forgive the young man who proclaims that honey is the labour of the bee. On this, Tzetzes, Chiliad 8, History 208: [III, 370] Τοῦτο τὸ σχῆμα γίνωσκε τυγχάνειν εἰρωνείας. Καὶ τίς γὰρ, ὃς ἠγνόηκε πόνον μελίσσης μέλι; [Touto to schēma ginōske tynchanein eirōneias. Kai tis gar, hos ēgnoēke ponon melissēs meli?]

Know that this figure is irony. For who is there who does not know that the labour of the bee is honey? Further, it is truly said that honey is used πρὸς ὑγίειαν [pros hygieian], for health. For so the ancients hold. Hippocrates, chapter 50 of On Affections: Μέλι, ξὺν ἑτέροις ἐσθιόμενον, καὶ τρέφει, καὶ εὔχροιαν παρέχει [Meli, xyn heterois esthiomenon, kai trephei, kai euchroian parechei]; Honey, eaten with other things, both nourishes and gives a good colour. And in chapter 54: Οἶνος καὶ μέλι κάλλιστα κέκριται ἐν ἀνθρώποισι, ἢν πρὸς φύσιν καὶ ὑγιαίνουσι, καὶ ἀσθενέουσι, σὺν καιρῷ, καὶ μετριότητι, προσφέρονται [Oinos kai meli kallista kekritai en anthrōpoisi, ēn pros physin kai hygiainousi, kai astheneousi, syn kairō, kai metriotēti, prospherontai]; Wine and honey have been judged best for human beings, if they are given in accordance with nature to both the healthy and the weak, at the right time and in moderation. Diophanes, book 15 of the Geoponica: Οὐ μόνον ἡδὺ τοῖς χρωμένοις, ἀλλὰ καὶ μακροβίους ποιεῖ· οἱ οὖν γήρᾳ μέλιτι μετὰ ἄρτου μόνου τρεφόμενοι, ἐπὶ πλεῖστον βιοῦσι· καὶ τὰς αἰσθήσεις δὲ διαφυλάττει πάσας ἐῤῥωμένας [Ou monon hēdy tois chrōmenois, alla kai makrobious poiei; hoi oun gēra meliti meta artou monou trephomenoi, epi pleiston biousi; kai tas aisthēseis de diaphylattei pasas errōmenas]. Honey is not only pleasant to those who use it, but also makes them long-lived. So those who in old age eat honey with bread alone live a long time; and that food keeps the senses vigorous. Accordingly, Λύκος πολυχρονίους φησὶν εἶναι τοὺς Κυρνίους, διὰ τὸ μέλιτι ἀεὶ χρῆσθαι [Lykos polychronious phēsin einai tous Kyrnious, dia to meliti aei chrēsthai]: Lycus reports that the Corsicans are long-lived, because they always use honey. So Athenaeus, book 2, chapter 7. And in the same place: Τῶν Πυθαγορικῶν τροφὴ ἄρτος μετὰ μέλιτος, ὥς φησι Ἀριστόξενος, τοὺς προσφερομένους αὐτὰ ἀεὶ ἐπ᾽ ἀρίστῳ λέγων ἀνόσως διατελεῖν [Tōn Pythagorikōn trophē artos meta melitos, hōs phēsi Aristoxenos, tous prospheromenous auta aei ep' aristō legōn anosōs diatelein]. Aristoxenus writes that the food of the Pythagoreans was bread with honey, adding that those who always take these at their midday meal live free of disease. They seem to have learned this from their teacher, Pythagoras, of whom Eustathius on Iliad λ᾽ [l']: Ὡς δὲ καὶ τρόφιμον τὸ μέλι Πυθαγορᾶς μαρτυρεῖ, ὃς, εὐτελέστατα διαβιοὺς, πολλάκις μέλιτι μόνῳ ἠρκεῖτο [Hōs de kai trophimon to meli Pythagoras martyrei, hos, eutelestata diabious, pollakis meliti monō ērkeito]. Pythagoras also testifies that honey can nourish; living very frugally, he was mostly content with honey alone. To the same effect is the old proverb about Glaucus, Γλαῦκος πινὼν μέλι ἀνέστη [Glaukos pinōn meli anestē]: Glaucus, having drunk honey, came back to life; that is, if I grasp the meaning of the Paroemiographer, he recovered from a grave illness. And Athenaeus writes of Democritus that, when he had already been given up for dead, διαζῆσαι ἡμέρας ἱκανὰς, τῇ ἀπὸ τοῦ μέλιτος ἀναφορᾷ μόνῃ τρεφόμενον [diazēsai hēmeras hikanas, tē apo tou melitos anaphora monē trephomenon], he prolonged his life for some days, nourished only by the smell of honey. For, as follows in the same place, he took the greatest delight in the use of honey. So Πρὸς τὸν πυθόμενον, Πῶς ἂν ὑγιῶς τις διάγοι; ἔφη, Εἰ τὰ μὲν ἐντὸς μέλιτι βρέχοι, τὰ δὲ ἐκτὸς ἐλαίῳ [Pros ton pythomenon, Pōs an hygiōs tis diagoi? ephē, Ei ta men entos meliti brechoi, ta de ektos elaiō]; [col. 515] to one who asked how a person might live his life in health, he replied: if the inner parts of the body were moistened with honey, the outer with oil. Not much differently Diophanes: Δημόκριτος δὲ, ἐρωτηθεὶς, Πῶς ἂν ἄνοσοι καὶ μακραίωνες γίγνοιντο οἱ ἄνθρωποι; εἶπεν, Εἰ τὰ μὲν ἔξωθεν ἐλαίῳ τοῦ σώματος, τὰ δὲ ἔνδοθεν μέλιτι [Dēmokritos de, erōtētheis, Pōs an anosoi kai makraiōnes gignointo hoi anthrōpoi? eipen, Ei ta men exōthen elaiō tou sōmatos, ta de endothen meliti] [III, 371] χρήσαιντο [chrēsainto]. For this I would prefer χρίσαιντο [chrisainto]. From the same source is drawn the saying of Pollio, of which Pliny, book 22, chapter 24: Many have sustained a long old age on the nourishment of mead alone, with no other food at all, as in the famous example of Pollio Romulus. When he was past his hundredth year, the Divine Augustus, his guest, asked him by what means above all he had preserved that vigour of mind and body. And he replied: within by mead, without by oil. Mulsum [mead], that is, τῷ οἰνομέλιτι [tō oinomeliti]. It is clear, then, that honey is rightly placed among the dishes of kings and great men. This is easily proved by examples taken from Scripture. Thus honey is sent as a choice gift to Joseph, viceroy of Egypt, Gen 43:11 and to King David, when he was in the town of Mahanaim, neighbouring nobles offered honey, 2 Sam 17:29 Solomon too speaks thus, Song 5:1. I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey. Not to mention Jonathan, the king's son, whose eyes and strength were restored by eating honey, 1 Sam 14:27. If we add profane sources to these, in Iliad λ΄ [l'], line 630, we shall find that Hecamede set before Nestor and Patroclus at a banquet μέλι χλωρὸν [meli chlōron], yellow honey, or fresh honey. And in Odyssey υ΄ [y'], line 69, that Venus nourished the daughters of Pandarus τυρῷ, καὶ μέλιτι γλυκερῷ [tyrō, kai meliti glykerō], with cheese and sweet honey. So Suetonius on Nero, chapter 27: He also imposed dinners on his friends, of which one cost four million sesterces for the honeyed dishes; that is, one hundred thousand gold pieces, by Budé's reckoning. But the word mellita [honeyed dishes], which the common editions have, the most learned Casaubon changed into mitellita, because the oldest manuscripts read so. Yet he candidly admits that he does not know what mitellita are. Today, since the invention of sugar, no one will be surprised that honey has lost much of its value. 7. It is added that the bee is ποθεινὴν καὶ ἐπίδοξον [potheinēn kai epidoxon], beloved and renowned, among all. For honey is produced everywhere, as Pliny notes, book 22, chapter 23, and it is valued everywhere, from farthest Scythia to the Africans and Ethiopians. Augustine, or whoever the author is, in Sermon 15 To the Brothers in the Desert, writes that the philosopher Aristodemus toiled for many years in investigating the nature of the bee. But for Aristodemus I would gladly write Aristomachus, of whom Pliny, book 11, chapter 9: Let no one wonder that men have been captivated by love of them (the bees), that Aristomachus of Soli did nothing else for fifty-eight years, while Philiscus of Thasos, who kept bees in the wilderness, was surnamed Agrius [the Wild]. 8. Finally, the conclusion is this: Although (the bee) is weak in strength, τὴν σοφίαν τιμήσασα προήχθη [tēn sophian timēsasa proēchthē], because she honoured wisdom (that is, through the pursuit of wisdom) she has been advanced. That is, as prudence is ascribed to the serpent, so the pursuit of wisdom is ascribed to the bee καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs], since she does by natural instinct what, if human beings did it, would rightly enrol them in the catalogue of the wise. By this καταχρήσει [katachrēsei] not a few write that the bee is wise. Thus Lucian in the Halcyon calls the bee σοφὴν θείου μέλιτος ἐργάτιν [sophēn theiou melitos ergatin], the wise maker of divine honey. And Plutarch, Περὶ φιλοστοργίας [Peri philostorgias]: Τὴν μέλιτταν ἡμεῖς σοφὴν καλοῦμεν, καὶ νομίζομεν, ξανθὸν μέλι μηδομένην [Tēn melittan hēmeis sophēn kaloumen, kai nomizomen, xanthon meli mēdomenēn]; We call and consider the bee wise [III, 372] because she produces yellow honey. Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], chapter 27, on the bee,
Ἡ σύντονος δ᾽ οὖν, καὶ σοφὴ, καὶ τεχνικὴ, [Hē syntonos d' oun, kai sophē, kai technikē,]
She, then, energetic, and wise, and skilled in craft. And in chapter 28,
Καὶ ζῇ μὲν ἁγνὸν ἡ σοφὴ σχεδὸν βίον, [Kai zē men hagnon hē sophē schedon bion,]
And the wise one is wont to live a pure life. Pisides, De mundi opificio, verse 137:

Τίς τὴν μέλιτταν τὴν σοφὴν τὴν ἐργάτιν [col. 516] Γεωμετρεῖν ἔπεισε, καὶ τριωρόφους Οἴκους ἐγείρειν ἑξαγώνων κτισμάτων; [Tis tēn melittan tēn sophēn tēn ergatin geōmetrein epeise, kai triōrophous oikous egeirein hexagōnōn ktismatōn?]
Who induced the wise, craftsmanlike bee to practise geometry, and to raise houses of three storeys in hexagonal construction? And further on,
Μή που σε κέντρον τῆς σοφῆς διδασκάλου Πλήξῃ μελίττης, καὶ μαθεῖν ἀναγκάσῃ· [Mē pou se kentron tēs sophēs didaskalou plēxē melittēs, kai mathein anankasē;]

Lest the sting of the bee, that wise teacher, strike you and compel you to learn. Didymus, in book 15 of the Geoponica: Ἡ μέλιττα πάντων τῶν λοιπῶν ζώων ἐστὶ σοφωτάτη, καὶ εὐμηχανωτάτη, καὶ σύνεγγυς ἀνθρώπῳ κατὰ τὸ συνετόν [Hē melitta pantōn tōn loipōn zōōn esti sophōtatē, kai eumēchanōtatē, kai synengys anthrōpō kata to syneton]: The bee is the wisest and most ingenious of all animals, and comes closest to the shrewdness of man. Finally the Poet, magnifying the matter in poetic fashion, held that bees have a share of the divine mind. His words are:
Following these signs and these examples, some have said that bees have a share of the divine mind and draughts of the ether. — — — —

The third passage on the honey-making of bees is taken from a book which neither survives in Hebrew nor is acknowledged as canonical by the Hebrews. The Greek words of Ecclesiasticus XI, 3. run thus: Μικρὰ ἐν πετεινοῖς μέλισσα, καὶ ἀρχὴ γλυκασμάτων ὁ καρπὸς αὐτῆς· [Mikra en peteinois melissa, kai archē glykasmatōn ho karpos autēs;] The bee is small among flying creatures, and her fruit is the beginning of sweet things. Small among flying creatures: that is, one of the smallest, not absolutely the smallest of flying creatures, as Drusius has it here. For the fly and the gnat are smaller than the bee. Thus Bethlehem was small among the thousands of Judah, yet not the least of all, Matt 2:6 The beginning of sweet things: that is, supremely sweet, holding first place among sweet things. As in Amos 6:6. ראשית שמנים, they anoint themselves with the beginning of ointments, that is, with the chief ointment. For the fruit of the bee, which is honey, holds first place among sweet things. Hence the Hebrew proverb, Sweet as honey, of which below. This verse about the bee must be joined with the one immediately preceding: Μὴ αἰνέσῃς ἄνδρα ἐν κάλλει αὐτοῦ, καὶ μὴ βδελύξῃ ἄνθρωπον ἐν ὁράσει αὐτοῦ [Mē ainesēs andra en kallei autou, kai mē bdelyxē anthrōpon en horasei autou]. Do not praise a man for his beauty [III, 373], nor disdain a man because of his appearance. By these words he does not mean that a man gains no recommendation from his looks; for
Virtue is more pleasing when it comes from a handsome body:

He means only that a man's praise does not chiefly lie in his being outstanding in form, since true praise consists not so much in goods of the body as in goods of the mind. Accordingly, no one is to be despised for his outward appearance, say, if he is rather ugly or short of stature. For often
Greater virtue has reigned in a slight body.

This is proved by the example of the bee, which, however small, yet produces a fruit of remarkable sweetness. Although this is the true meaning of the author, nevertheless Epiphanius, in the Physiologus, chapter 21, understood the same passage quite differently, as his words show: It is said by the wise man: the bee is small among flying creatures, and her fruit is the beginning of sweet things. So too the works of God are ἀνεξιχνίαστα ἐν ἀνθρώποις, καὶ θαυμαστὰ ἐν ὑψηλοῖς, καὶ γλυκύτερα ὑπὲρ μέλι [anexichniasta en anthrōpois, kai thaumasta en hypsēlois, kai glykytera hyper meli], inscrutable among men, and wonderful in the heights, and sweeter than honey. This is partly drawn from verse 5 of the same Sirach: Ὅτι θαυμαστὰ τὰ ἔργα Κυρίου, καὶ κρυπτὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀνθρώποις· [Hoti thaumasta ta erga Kyriou, kai krypta ta erga autou en anthrōpois;] as if that fifth verse were connected with the third, which is about the bee. But it is connected with the fourth, immediately preceding, in which he had told man not to boast, and that there is no reason for him to exalt himself when he is honoured by others. For God, whose works (that is, judgements) are wonderful and inscrutable, can in a single moment cast the proud down from their station and drive them to ruin, as befell Nebuchadnezzar, Dan 4:31 and Herod, Acts 12:23. That this is the true sense of the passage is confirmed by what follows in verses 6 and 7 about tyrants brought down to the ground, the mighty covered with disgrace, and the illustrious delivered into the hands of others.
